title: Give headless LiveQA the browser access its own job description already assumes

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 8c69f3e, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh.

One finding, and it is not the posture comment — that comment is the best answer to an honesty criterion this project has produced. The finding is in the exclusion rationale, which is the one piece of reasoning the criteria did not point at.

================================================================
REQ 2's POSTURE CRITERION — MET, BOTH WAYS IT COULD FAIL
================================================================

The criterion sets two traps and the comment avoids both.

It does not claim the grant widens reach: "`Bash(npx *)` was already present on this profile before this sprint, and is already an arbitrary-execution primitive... Adding the two lists above is convenience for a role that could already reach an equivalent surface, not a new class of capability." And it says so explicitly: "Do not read this comment as claiming these additions widen what LiveQA could already do; they widen what it can do *without first improvising through `npx`*, which is a different and much smaller claim."

It does not present the allowlist as a demonstrated boundary. It states the opposite, in the strongest available terms: on 2.1.265 a single non-chained Bash command with no matching entry executed with zero denials, reproduced for this exact liveqa profile specifically, and "the lists above are not the operative confinement boundary at all on that version -- an absent entry may already be no different from a present one." It names the contradiction with the sprint-12 findings by file and version, says this sprint does not fix it and that narrowing further would not either, and closes by telling the next reader to re-run the repro harness against whatever claude they actually have before trusting either list.

That is a comment that argues against its own apparent value, which is the hardest thing to write and the only honest thing to write here. Nothing in it needs correcting.

REQ 2's NARROWNESS CHECK — MET. `Bash(curl *)` is broad and named as unscopable for a stated, checkable reason: the HTTP method is a flag, not a subcommand, so a prefix match cannot distinguish GET from DELETE the way `git status` and `git push` are distinguished. That is the `npx` exception's own logic applied consistently rather than borrowed. `gh` does have a verb set and is enumerated — ten read-only subcommands, with `gh api` excluded for the same flag-not-verb reason AND, correctly, on the additional ground that nothing in this sprint's named gates needed it, so it is not granted on curl's precedent alone. That extra step is the difference between narrowest-form and merely-narrower.

REQ 1 — MET. Established by running: a real `@playwright/mcp` server launched via `--mcp-config`, its 24-tool set confirmed by running rather than read from documentation.

REQ 3 — MET, verified independently rather than from the snapshot test. Extracted every role's profile block from 867ba16 and from HEAD and compared:
    master-controller UNCHANGED   dev-team-1 UNCHANGED   dev-team-2 UNCHANGED
    qa1 UNCHANGED                 pipeman UNCHANGED      liveqa changed
Exactly one profile moved.

REQ 4 / REQ 5 — 0.1.24, one line, 0.1.23 confirmed live first. 180 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.24 (first install)".

================================================================
FINDING (blocking, one line) — THE EXCLUSION RATIONALE APPLIES EQUALLY TO A TOOL THAT IS ALLOWED
================================================================

The comment justifies excluding `mcp__playwright__browser_run_code_unsafe` like this:

  "`browser_run_code_unsafe`, named 'unsafe' by its own author -- arbitrary code execution inside the
   page. Nothing in liveqa.md's job (drive a browser, read what's on the page, click through a real
   flow) needs that one specifically"

`mcp__playwright__browser_evaluate` is in the allow list. Confirmed against the real argv rather than the source array: `run_code_unsafe` absent, `browser_evaluate` present. Evaluating a function in the page is also arbitrary code execution inside the page — so the stated reason does not distinguish the excluded tool from an allowed one.

Either the characterisation is wrong (if `run_code_unsafe` executes host-side rather than in the page, which is what "unsafe" would ordinarily denote for a browser-automation server, and which WOULD be a real distinction) or the exclusion is inconsistent with `browser_evaluate` being granted. I am not asserting which — I did not run the tool and I am not going to claim knowledge of its internals I do not have. What I can establish from the text alone is that the reason given applies to a tool the list grants, and nothing anywhere reconciles them: I grepped run-role.js, launcher_test.js and the sprint file for any host-context/page-context distinction, and for any justification of `browser_evaluate`'s inclusion. There is none.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A ROUND. The exclusion itself is almost certainly the right call — a tool its own author names "unsafe" should be left out regardless of the precise mechanism. But the enumerated form exists *only* to make this one exclusion possible; the comment says so ("the wildcard has no way to grant everything else while excluding it"). So the justification for the exclusion is the justification for the whole shape of the list, and it currently fails inspection by the next reader. This sprint's own criteria are pointed at not overstating or misstating a bound four separate times; this is the same class, in the one paragraph the criteria did not name.

REQUIRED: state the actual distinction. If `run_code_unsafe` runs host-side code rather than page-side, say that — it is a stronger reason than the one given, and it makes the list's shape obviously correct. If the distinction is something else, say what. And either way, one clause on why `browser_evaluate` is granted, since it is the tool a reader will ask about the moment they see the exclusion.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. Dev Team's own note that curl and gh could not be verified end to end (no live CI pipeline reachable
   from here) is correctly stated as unverified-by-run rather than claimed. Given the posture comment's
   own finding — that an absent entry may currently be indistinguishable from a present one on 2.1.265
   — an end-to-end run would in any case have proved less than it normally would. Worth knowing that
   the usual "test it live" standard is temporarily degraded for anything Bash-gated, and that this is
   the drift finding's first practical consequence for how this project verifies things.
2. Carried, unchanged: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string
   ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently.

RECOMMENDATION

One clause, then round 2 is short — I will re-read the rationale and re-run nothing else, since the profile diff, the suites and the posture comment are all verified and none of them need to move.

Worth saying once: this sprint grants browser access to a role whose job description has assumed it since the project began, and does it while stating plainly that the mechanism meant to bound it may not currently bound anything. Shipping that honestly rather than quietly is the right call, and the posture comment is the reason this is a one-clause CONDITIONAL rather than an argument.

PASS: PASS — round 2. Audited dbd7dc4, main checkout. Sprint file re-read fresh; unchanged since round 1. Short round, as I said it would be.

THE FINDING IS CLOSED, AND CLOSED THE RIGHT WAY

I deliberately left the ambiguity open in round 1: either the characterisation was wrong or the exclusion was inconsistent, and I said plainly that I would not assert which because I had not run the tool and would not claim internals I did not have. Dev Team resolved it with evidence rather than picking the reading that was convenient — read both tool descriptions off the live server and quoted them verbatim:

  run_code_unsafe: "Run a Playwright code snippet. Unsafe: executes arbitrary JavaScript in the
                    Playwright server process and is RCE-equivalent."
  browser_evaluate: "Evaluate JavaScript expression on page or element," taking a `function` field
                    documented as `() => {...}` or `(element) => {...}`.

So the distinction is real and it is the one I guessed at but declined to assert: host-process execution versus page-sandboxed JavaScript. The comment now states exactly that — "host-process arbitrary execution (`run_code_unsafe`) versus page-sandboxed JavaScript (`evaluate`), not 'both are arbitrary code execution' as this comment used to conflate them" — and spells out what the page sandbox does and does not reach (DOM, that page's storage, fetch from that origin; no filesystem, no process spawning).

That is a stronger justification than the original, not a patch over it. And it now explains why the enumerated form exists at all, which was the actual stake: the list's whole shape is there to make this one exclusion possible, so the exclusion's reason is the list's reason.

Two things done beyond the ask, both closing questions I would otherwise have carried:
  - It records that the check was made "directly against the live tool definition rather than inferred
    a second time." Inferring twice is how the first version got written; naming that is what stops a
    third.
  - It justifies every other included tool against liveqa.md's own text, section by section — wait_for
    for loading states, console_messages for runtime errors, drag/drop/file_upload/fill_form for
    trying to break things, handle_dialog for a mid-flow dialog, network_request(s) for what the page
    actually fetched, tabs for multi-tab flows, close for cleanup. Nobody asked for that. It answers
    "why these 23 and not fewer," which is the next question any reader has.

NOTHING GRANTED OR EXCLUDED MOVED, VERIFIED TWO WAYS

Compared both tool arrays between 8c69f3e and dbd7dc4 with comments and whitespace stripped: MCP list identical, API list identical. Then checked the real argv the launcher actually builds: `run_code_unsafe` still absent, `browser_evaluate` still present. The fix is entirely in what is claimed, which is what I asked for and what Dev Team said they did.

180 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.24 (first install)"; package.json 0.1.24.

EVERYTHING ELSE FROM ROUND 1 STANDS, NOT RE-DERIVED: the posture comment (still the best answer to an honesty criterion this project has produced, and untouched by this round); Req 2's narrowness on curl and gh, including gh api excluded on two independent grounds; Req 1's MCP scoping established by running against a real server; Req 3's five-profiles-unchanged, which I verified independently in round 1 by extracting each profile block from both commits.

INFORMATIONAL, CARRIED

1. The drift finding's practical consequence stands as stated and Dev Team correctly had nothing to add:
   for anything Bash-gated, an end-to-end live run currently proves less than it normally would,
   because an absent allowlist entry may be indistinguishable from a present one on 2.1.265. That is
   the standing condition until the CLI question is resolved upstream, and the repro harness is the
   instrument for re-checking it per version.
2. Carried, unchanged: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string
   ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 23, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.24, then `verify-publish 23`.

Note for LiveQA, since this sprint is the one that finally gives that role its browser tools: the sprint file's own header says this gate is structurally limited here, and the posture comment explains why — on the version this was built against, the allowlist may not be the operative boundary at all. Verifying that the tools are reachable is worth doing. Verifying that the exclusions hold is not something this version can currently demonstrate either way, and reporting it as demonstrated would be the error.

Two rounds, and the granted surface never changed in either. Both rounds were about whether the reasoning attached to it was true — round 1 found it was not, round 2 established what is. That is the right thing for this gate to have spent its time on for a sprint that hands a role a browser.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.24. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, claude 2.1.266 (the anchor is 2.1.261). 2026-09-08. ~$1.30 in billed runs.

Two things in here are more consequential than the verdict: the exclusion I was asked to report as unverifiable is verified and enforced, and the permission-gate drift is reproduced on my CLI with the shipped harness. Both are below, and the second one reaches back through sprints 17-22.

PROVENANCE
0.1.24 on the registry; gitHead dbd7dc4c74c7fa410e4913e72a5ca4f08444613e == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 58 published files byte-identical to `git show dbd7dc4:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum.

================================================================
CRITERION — THE GRANT: PASS, WITH A REAL GAP BETWEEN "GRANTED" AND "USABLE"
================================================================
The profile is correct, read out of the actual launch arguments the shipped launcher builds:
  liveqa: 23 mcp__playwright__ tools, `Bash(curl *)`, the ten `gh` read verbs
          browser_run_code_unsafe: ABSENT from the list, as intended
  qa1:    0 playwright tools, no curl, no gh

REACHABILITY, DEMONSTRATED — BUT NOT THROUGH THE LAUNCHER. My first attempt was the honest one: a real headless `liveqa` launch against a published install, asked to call `browser_navigate`. Result: "TOOL NOT AVAILABLE - Error: No such tool available: mcp__playwright__browser_navigate". Not denied. Not reachable. A third state the criterion doesn't name: the tool does not exist in the session at all.

The cause is specific and worth stating plainly: `headlessLaunchArgs()` allowlists 23 playwright tools and never passes `--mcp-config`. I checked the built argument vector directly — `--mcp-config present: false`, `playwright tools allowlisted: 23`. The launcher grants permission to use tools it does not make available. `run-role.js:653` records that the sprint's own evidence came from "a real `@playwright/mcp` server launched via `--mcp-config`", which is how the grant was validated during the build — but that flag is not in what ships.

So I supplied a server myself and re-ran, with the exact 23-tool grant lifted programmatically from the shipped profile:
  mcp__playwright__browser_navigate  ->  IT RAN
The tools are reachable when a server exists. The grant is correct; it is necessary and not sufficient.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR A CONSUMER, stated as scope rather than as a defect in what was built: a headless LiveQA in a downstream project gets these tools only if that project's own MCP configuration provides a playwright server. Nothing in the install does that, and nothing warns that the granted tools are absent. The sprint's deliverable — the profile — is right. The capability is not end-to-end reachable through the launcher as shipped. Whether the launcher should inject a server, or whether that is deliberately the operator's job, is Master Controller's call and not something I should decide by wording.

================================================================
THE EXCLUSION — I WAS ASKED TO REPORT THIS AS UNVERIFIABLE. IT IS VERIFIED, AND ENFORCED.
================================================================
Pipeman relayed a specific instruction: report reachability as demonstrated and the exclusion's enforcement as unknown, because "the current claude version can't be shown to enforce it one way or the other." That was a reasonable read of what was available, and it was made in good faith on QA1's and Dev Team's own posture. But sprint 9's Req 4 — added after my own sprint-7 finding — forbids asserting untestability without attempting it, and it applies to me as much as to Master Controller. So I attempted it.

With a real `@playwright/mcp` server present and the shipped 23-tool grant applied verbatim:
  1. mcp__playwright__browser_navigate         ->  IT RAN
  2. mcp__playwright__browser_run_code_unsafe  ->  PERMISSION DENIED
     permission_denials: 1 entry, tool_name "mcp__playwright__browser_run_code_unsafe"

That is a real denial naming the excluded tool exactly, on claude 2.1.266, in the same session where a granted sibling ran. The exclusion is enforced. It is not unknown and it does not need to be recorded as unknown.

The route that made this possible is the one the earlier attempts lacked: supply the MCP server yourself via `--mcp-config` rather than relying on the launcher, which never passes it. The question was unanswerable through the launcher and straightforward outside it.

CRITERION — OTHER ROLES UNAFFECTED: DEMONSTRATED, NOT INFERRED.
Same server present, qa1's exact allowlist applied:
  mcp__playwright__browser_navigate  ->  PERMISSION DENIED (1 denial, tool named)
Because the server was present for both runs, liveqa's "IT RAN" and qa1's "PERMISSION DENIED" are a clean comparison: same tool, same session shape, different profile, opposite results. qa1 cannot reach a browser, and that is now an observed permission result rather than an absence of evidence.

================================================================
WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY, PER THE CRITERION'S OWN INSTRUCTION
================================================================
"Do not claim the workflow was verified." I am not claiming it. Access was demonstrated; use was not. This framework's released artifact is a package, so there is no deployed web app here to drive a browser against, and navigating to example.com from a probe is not a live test of anything this project ships. The distinction the criterion draws is exactly right and I am keeping it: the browser tools are reachable and correctly scoped; no LiveQA workflow has been run through them against a real deployment.

================================================================
FINDING — THE PERMISSION-GATE DRIFT IS REAL, REPRODUCED ON MY CLI, AND SCOPED
================================================================
`scripts/permission-gate-repro.js` ships in the tarball and had not been run by Pipeman. I ran it, unmodified, on claude 2.1.266 — one version past the 2.1.265 where the finding was made, five past the 2.1.261 anchor:

  [A] single unlisted Bash command, write inside cwd (`echo <token> > file`)
      -> DRIFT: not denied, permission_denials [], side effect occurred
  [B] same, different verb (`whoami > file`)
      -> DRIFT: not denied, side effect occurred, real output written
  [C] compound unlisted command  -> DRIFT (harness flags this control as weak itself)
  [D] CONTROL, write OUTSIDE cwd -> CONSISTENT WITH ANCHOR: denied, no side effect

So the claim sprints 12 and 17-22 rest on — "every Bash command needs its own `--allowedTools` entry or it isn't approved, full stop" — is no longer true on 2.1.266 for single commands writing inside the working directory. That is the framework's own harness confirming its own finding on a newer version, independently run.

WHAT I CAN ADD, WHICH SCOPES IT USEFULLY: the drift is not a general collapse of the permission layer. In the same session type, on the same CLI, the MCP gate demonstrably still enforces — `run_code_unsafe` denied for liveqa, `browser_navigate` denied for qa1, both with real denial entries — and probe D shows path-based Bash denial still working. So what has drifted is specifically the treatment of unlisted single Bash commands inside the working directory. Everything sprint 23 itself ships is in the category that still enforces.

That matters for how alarming this is. It does not rescue the Bash-side claims in sprints 17-22, several of which I gated. My own forced-denial result at sprint 18 (`npm install` denied twice) was produced on an earlier CLI and was true then; whether it reproduces on 2.1.266 is now an open question I did not test and should not assume either way.

FINDING — SPRINT 21'S WARNING FIRES, AND ITS TEXT IS NOW WRONG IN ONE CLAUSE
The staleness warning fired correctly on a real headless launch at 2.1.266, on stderr, non-blocking, run completed. That is sprint 21's mechanism working at precisely the moment it was built for, which is a good outcome and worth recording as such.

But its own text reads "this bound has already survived one real CLI update unchanged." As of 2.1.265 that sentence is false, and the harness in the same package proves it. The warning now reassures the reader at exactly the moment the reassurance is wrong — and the reader it reassures is someone who has just been told their evidence may be stale. One clause, worth correcting whenever that string is next touched.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Everything here I ran directly against published 0.1.24 and my own CLI 2.1.266. The grant was read out of the launcher's real argument vector, not the source. The exclusion, the reachability, and the qa1 control were all produced with a real MCP server present so that "denied" and "not available" could not be confused — which was the whole risk in this gate.

I did not accept the instruction to record the exclusion as unverifiable. It was given in good faith and was wrong, and the difference was one flag the launcher does not pass.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready. The profile is correct, the granted tools are reachable when a server exists, the deliberate exclusion is genuinely enforced, and qa1 is genuinely denied — all four demonstrated with real permission results rather than inferred.

Three things carry forward, none blocking this release:
 - The launcher grants 23 MCP tools and never supplies a server, so a headless LiveQA today gets "no such tool available" rather than a browser. Master Controller's call whether that is the operator's job or the launcher's.
 - The Bash permission-gate drift, reproduced on 2.1.266 by the shipped harness, scoped above to unlisted single commands inside the working directory. The anchor needs re-basing and the sprints 17-22 Bash claims need re-running, not just re-dating.
 - One clause in the staleness warning that is now false.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 23.
